# National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM)
Established on September 22, 1910, by Justo Sierra, UNAM replaced Mexico's Royal and Pontifical University with a secular, nationally focused institution. It unified various decentralized colleges in Mexico City, adopting a liberal educational philosophy amidst political challenges like the Mexican Revolution. After years of struggle, the university gained autonomy in the 1920s, with its rector becoming the final authority over policies and curriculum. The main campus, Ciudad Universitaria, constructed in the 1950s in southern Mexico City, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007. UNAM has since expanded through multiple metropolitan and regional satellite campuses aimed at research and graduate studies.
UNAM is organized into a system of schools and colleges offering undergraduate to doctoral degrees, including both national schools focused on undergraduate practical training and graduate-oriented faculties. It supports one of the largest student bodies globally, exceeding 324,000 students, including high schools under its preparatory system. Renowned for research, it houses numerous institutes covering astronomy, biotechnology, nuclear sciences, ecology, physics, engineering, and more, maintaining international competitiveness despite limited national R&D funding. UNAM actively promotes minority inclusion and has notable cultural landmarks such as the Palacio de Minería, Casa del Lago, and several museums integral to Mexican heritage. Its alumni and faculty include Nobel laureates, influential politicians, artists, scientists, and business leaders, highlighting its broad impact on Mexico and Latin America.
